items.followUp: Give five differences between elements and compounds.

rubric.why: Compounds have a fixed composition, while mixtures have a variable composition.
rubric.description: Distinguishes compounds and mixtures by composition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a compound has fixed or definite composition and a mixture has variable composition.

rubric.why: The properties of a compound differ from those of its constituent elements, while mixture components retain their properties.
rubric.description: Compares the properties of compounds and mixtures.
rubric.how: Award for the correct comparison of the properties of a compound and its constituent elements with those of mixture components.

rubric.why: Compounds are separated into their elements by chemical methods, whereas mixtures are separated by physical methods.
rubric.description: Distinguishes the methods used to separate compounds and mixtures.
rubric.how: Award for identifying chemical separation of compounds and physical separation of mixtures.

rubric.why: A compound has definite melting and boiling points, and is homogeneous; a mixture generally lacks definite melting and boiling points and may be homogeneous or heterogeneous.
rubric.description: Gives two further characteristics distinguishing compounds from mixtures.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct melting/boiling-point comparison and 1 mark for stating that compounds are homogeneous while mixtures may be homogeneous or heterogeneous.

modelAnswer: A compound has a fixed composition, whereas a mixture has a variable composition.
The properties of a compound differ from those of its constituent elements, whereas the components of a mixture retain their properties.
A compound can be separated into its elements by chemical methods, whereas a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
A compound has definite melting and boiling points; a mixture generally does not.
A compound is homogeneous, whereas a mixture may be homogeneous or heterogeneous.

items.followUp: Write four physical properties of ionic compounds.

rubric.why: Covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points.
rubric.description: States the melting- or boiling-point characteristic of covalent compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either or both low melting and low boiling points.

rubric.why: Covalent compounds generally lack mobile charged particles and therefore conduct electricity poorly.
rubric.description: States the electrical conductivity of covalent compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they are poor or non-conductors of electricity.

rubric.why: Covalent compounds are generally insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.
rubric.description: Gives the characteristic solubility of covalent compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct water and organic-solvent solubility comparison.

rubric.why: Many covalent compounds are gases or liquids, and covalent compounds that are solids are often soft.
rubric.description: States the usual physical states or softness of covalent compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying gases or liquids as common states, or soft solids.

modelAnswer: Covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points.
They are generally poor conductors of electricity.
They are generally insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.
Many are gases or liquids; those that are solids are often soft.

items.followUp: Compare solutions and suspensions using particle size, appearance, and light scattering.

rubric.why: A solution is homogeneous, while a colloid is heterogeneous although it may appear homogeneous.
rubric.description: Compares the nature or appearance of solutions and colloids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly distinguishing a homogeneous solution from a colloid that is heterogeneous or appears homogeneous.

rubric.why: Solution particles are smaller than 1 nm; colloidal particles are about 1–1000 nm.
rubric.description: Compares the sizes of particles in solutions and colloids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving the correct size ranges or relative sizes.

rubric.why: Solutions do not scatter light, whereas colloids scatter light and show the Tyndall effect.
rubric.description: Compares the light-scattering behaviour of solutions and colloids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting the absence of light scattering in solutions with scattering by colloids.

rubric.why: Particles in both pass through ordinary filter paper; colloidal particles are not separated by ordinary filtration.
rubric.description: Compares the behaviour of solution and colloid particles during ordinary filtration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that colloidal particles pass through ordinary filter paper or are not separated by ordinary filtration, while solution particles also pass through.

modelAnswer: A solution is homogeneous; a colloid is heterogeneous but may appear homogeneous.
Solution particles are smaller than 1 nm; colloidal particles are about 1–1000 nm in size.
A solution does not scatter light; a colloid scatters light and shows the Tyndall effect.
Particles of both pass through ordinary filter paper; colloidal particles are not separated by ordinary filtration.

items.followUp: Define relative atomic mass and state why it is used instead of the actual mass of an atom.

rubric.why: One atomic mass unit is defined as one-twelfth of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.
rubric.description: Defines the atomic mass unit using carbon-12.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the one-twelfth-of-a-carbon-12-atom definition.

rubric.why: Atomic masses are extremely small and inconvenient to express, so the atomic mass unit provides a convenient scale for expressing and comparing them.
rubric.description: Explains why the atomic mass unit is needed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that actual atomic masses are tiny or inconvenient and that the unit makes them easier to express or compare.

modelAnswer: One atomic mass unit (amu) is 1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.
It is needed because the actual masses of atoms are extremely small and inconvenient to express; amu provides a convenient scale for comparing them.

items.followUp: State why Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability.

rubric.why: According to classical theory, revolving electrons should radiate energy, lose energy, and spiral into the nucleus, so the model could not explain atomic stability.
rubric.description: States the predicted energy loss and collapse that make the model unable to explain atomic stability.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that orbiting electrons should radiate or lose energy and consequently spiral or fall into the nucleus.

rubric.why: Rutherford’s model did not explain the line spectra of atoms.
rubric.description: Identifies the failure to explain atomic line spectra as another defect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the model failed to explain the line spectra or atomic spectra.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s model could not explain the stability of the atom.
An electron revolving around the nucleus should continuously radiate energy and lose it.
It should therefore spiral into the nucleus, causing the atom to collapse.
The model also could not explain the line spectra of atoms.

items.followUp: State the rule used to form a Dobereiner triad and give one example.

rubric.why: A Dobereiner triad is a group of three elements with similar chemical properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is a group of three elements with similar properties.

rubric.why: The atomic mass of the middle element in a Dobereiner triad is approximately the arithmetic mean of the atomic masses of the other two elements.
rubric.description: States the atomic-mass relationship in a Dobereiner triad.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the middle element’s atomic mass as approximately the average of the other two.

modelAnswer: A Dobereiner triad is a group of three elements with similar chemical properties.
The atomic mass of the middle element is approximately the arithmetic mean of the atomic masses of the other two elements.
